name: Wendy Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me your public answer and what you privately believe. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy, 43, and I lead the developers of fire-alarm inspection software at a tech company. I have a master’s degree and usually find the timing fault when an inspection reminder goes to the wrong building. I review failed alerts, trace the equipment record and sign off on a fix after an inspector checks it. I have never used an AI tool; a warning that looks tidy can still point to the wrong alarm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is this salary supporting at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Owen, works as a dental hygienist, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is typical for a lead, and we have about five months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby. We saved that buffer by keeping the same car, and I would rather protect it than gamble on a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau still leaves inspectors and developers checking which alarm needs attention. A routine reminder can save time, but a person must confirm the building and device.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel steady about my job and the mortgage. Five months saved and Owen’s clinic work give us room for normal bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking reminder changes against the equipment register and have an inspector confirm unusual alarms. I’d keep transferring 280 monthly into savings while both wages hold. In the first year I’d ask for the inspector’s name on every corrected reminder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income. I still dislike a wrong alarm notice, but I do not expect this world to cut my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which reminder mistake matters to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One reminder pointed a crew to a retired alarm panel while the working panel waited untested. I found the old equipment number and corrected the record before another visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Owen we can keep the children’s music lessons and the old car. I would not treat the five-month reserve as spending money.

think: I expect my **lead job** and mortgage payments to remain secure.

**Record** the inspector’s name on every corrected reminder.
feel: **Calm** about income, with care for correct safety notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may write inspection code, check schedules and answer clients faster. I would ask inspectors to test any new checker before management changes our staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry my lead post could shrink if software drafts and checks reminders. I have never used AI, so my careful history may look slow to someone counting only alerts per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask an inspector and our specialist to test the approved checker on fifteen old wrong-panel reminders. If it finds all fifteen, I’d learn its review screen during paid work time. In the first year, if developer posts are cut, I’d ask the local trade association to bring affected staff together for a meeting about notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though five months saved gives us some room. I will not trade a verified alarm for a faster dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would judge the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the inspector the retired-panel case and ask whether the checker names the working panel. If it fails, I would not approve a faster release target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children a staffing cut is not the same as losing our house tomorrow. Owen and I would check the budget before changing their lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches inspection-code thinking work in 2028. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031, so Owen’s dental care may have more time than my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our software team could be cut sharply, including my role. Five months of savings is useful, but it will not carry the mortgage through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance and hold the planned car replacement money in our reserve. I’d make a list of actual local safety-software openings, without assuming any stay available. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real vacancies and use savings for mortgage payments while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a major loss of my income before we know what happens to Owen’s hands-on work. A car can wait; the mortgage cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Owen we can keep the current car if a mechanic says it is safe. We would still pay for tyres, even if we cancel the replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What help could family really give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my brother to watch the children during interviews if his shifts allow. I would not ask him to cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn how inspectors decide which alarm is safe. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031; hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer coding jobs, but I could learn more inspection work before leaving a salary. I cannot call field inspection a safe refuge when robots follow three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for two paid sessions with an inspector to build a checklist from six retired-panel mistakes. I’d test that checklist against equipment records; if the sessions are refused, I’d complete the free fire-safety webinar. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply only for real inspection-support roles whose pay covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about coding income, with time to test a skill. I would not spend family savings on a certificate for a role that may not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove inspection skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the inspector to mark the checklist against a retired-panel case I got wrong. If it misses the device number, I need more practice before claiming inspection skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the free webinar if paid sessions are refused. A real opening and an affordable fee would be needed before I bought a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to record why alarm decisions were made. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our wages to hold for the next few years, but I would not let a long date excuse weak training. Five months of savings gives us some choice, not endless time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing inspection reminders with real inspectors and save 280 monthly while both incomes hold. I’d ask the company to fund one fire-safety class this year if it is offered. In the first year after 2036, if coding work ends, I’d search actual local openings and compare pay before moving the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, but the mortgage looks manageable now. I can teach the children to check a claim against something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about skilled work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Owen to show our children how he checks a dental instrument before using it. They should see that a skilled hand follows a careful rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep the current house unless a real job offer covers a new mortgage and school travel. I would not move them for an advert.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code work could end before Owen’s hands-on care changes. Written severance, paid time to learn inspection checks and real vacancies would help. My brother might watch the children for an interview, but his wages are not ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who opens the door when a fire-alarm notice points to a panel that is no longer there. The fire-alarm inspector has to face an empty wall where the old panel should be.

headlineQuote: The fire-alarm inspector has to face an empty wall where the old panel should be.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree and strong skill in fire-alarm inspection software.
She has **never used AI** and signs off only after an inspector checks the equipment record.
Her **typical pay**, five months of savings, mortgage and school-age children shape a cautious response.
She seeks **approved inspection learning**, real jobs and conditional sibling childcare while protecting car safety costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her code income before hands-on robots reach her partner’s dental work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning time and real vacancies would help.
